rewrites.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of the region's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by the country's LGBT organisations documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. The capital has a visible, organised community.

If a trans visitor is arrested, the consequence axis is largely undocumented: the 2024 shadow report — the only prison-axis source in this record — contains no data on where trans prisoners are housed in the country (nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice). Its closest custody finding is the June 2024 case of a transgender woman attacked by police because of her gender identity, physically injured, arbitrarily detained and subjected to degrading treatment (under investigation by the judicial military police; police custody, no prison-placement information). In a legal system with no gender recognition and under-investigated violence, an undocumented placement practice cannot be assumed safe: what is on record is police violence against a trans person in custody.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised and sexual-orientation discrimination prohibited — of direct concern mainly to trans visitors who have relationships or are perceived as same-sex-active while travelling.

Legal context: the 2020 Penal Code that decriminalised same-sex conduct also criminalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment — a statutory sanction the same 2024 report documents as failing to stop persistent discrimination in health, education and employment.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Trans people have no legal gender recognition; the implementation gap (health, education, employment discrimination, under-investigated violence) falls on residents.

The June 2024 incident is a residents' case: a transgender woman attacked by police because of her gender identity, physically injured, arbitrarily detained by a local police station and subjected to degrading treatment, with the case under investigation by the judicial military police — police custody with no prison-placement information produced.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Statutory protections vs implementation gap documented by the country's civil-society organisations.

Prison axis: no rule, case or practice is documented on trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement finding, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice; the June 2024 case ended in police custody rather than prison placement, and what happens to trans people held after charge is unrecorded in these sources.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution. The constitutional court struck down the buggery and gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: an international human-rights organisation's profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026') contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement — no birth-sex vs identity rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice — in a country with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute, where the profile itself records transgender people as particularly vulnerable because no legal gender recognition mechanism exists; a detained trans visitor would face a prison system with no documented housing standard for trans people, and the absence of any rule cannot be read as a protected one.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The 2022 decriminalisation ruling covers same-sex conduct — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a partner; the criminal statutes no longer apply to anyone.

Litigation and legal-flux context: the 2022 ruling struck down Sections 12 and 15 of a 1995 sexual-offences act and read the constitutional bar on sex discrimination as inclusive of sexual orientation and gender identity; same-sex unions remain unrecognised, so partner-related protection stops at criminal-law neutrality, and no explicit anti-discrimination protections have followed the ruling.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
No legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute — resident-facing gaps.

For residents the gaps are concrete: there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers (only name changes), and the profile records transgender people as particularly vulnerable because of that absence.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Decriminalisation is recent; social climate lags the courts.

Prison axis: no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity), special units or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record; the gap cannot be read as safe in a country with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under national sex-discrimination law since 2013, and in August 2024 a landmark national-court ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. Subnational units have modernised rapidly: one strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and another passed a wide-ranging equality-legislation amendment (2024). There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the 2024 case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in this country; national research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a court granted a trans woman a protective order against an anti-trans activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented for one subnational unit: under a 2022 detention-oversight act (fully in force 2023) and its August 2023 inspection standards, transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender — identity-based placement — but staff still hold discretion at admission, and only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process; the 2009 corrections-service procedure this oversight replaced was assessed as largely ineffective. Placement practice in the other subnational units is not detailed in the current sources.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Adjacent context: the national legal trend is settled and protective — national sex-discrimination protection (2013), the 2024 national-court reading of it, and rapid subnational modernisation — while the live policy pressure documented nationally is the organised exclusionary campaign landscape (facilities and records-access disputes, rights-rollback pressures).

History and framing: decriminalisation across subnational units unfolded over decades from laws inherited from the historic metropole (one state/province kept the death penalty until 1949), and the national protections debate includes an ongoing terminological dispute over whether intersex people belong inside the same framework — framing, not visitor-facing risk. A national hate-crime offence (2025) and conversion-therapy bans covering most of the population (2024) extend the protective layer beyond the earlier baseline.

Policy evolution behind the placement standard: the 2009 corrections-service procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective (2009 law-student review), and oversight shifted to the 2022 detention-oversight act — institutional history rather than a visitor-facing risk.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Subnational legal gender recognition remains a patchwork (only some jurisdictions are self-declaration) and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing.

Resident-facing discrimination data from the sources: a 2003 research brief documented trans people's difficulties with sex designations on identity documents (passports, licences and birth certificates), high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places; the 2024 subnational-law modernisations govern residents, not visitors.

The subnational custody rules are resident-facing: placement by lived or experienced gender with staff discretion at admission and a surgery exception governs prisoners, not visitors; a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Subnational legal gender recognition patchwork and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing; the current sources do not assess marriage or partner-travel questions beyond the 2017 marriage-equality baseline, and border-document screening practice for visitors is not detailed.

Unverifiable in the current sources: three of the seven listed sources were not retrievable at research time (access denied; page removed; assembly bill text), including the 2024 discrimination ruling report and a subnational bill text; the remaining assessment of organised campaigns rests on the research brief alone.

Prison axis: the placement finding covers a single subnational unit and rests on a single section of an online-encyclopaedia survey; no data in these sources documents trans-prisoner housing in the other subnational units, special units, or solitary/segregation practice, and how the surgery exclusion is applied in practice is not documented.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution. The appeals court struck down the sodomy law in 2016 — the region's first decriminalisation ruling; the country has an organised community and anti-discrimination employment protection. No LGR; gang violence in the main city is a general risk.

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: the one prison-axis source in this record — an online-encyclopaedia survey of LGBTQ people in prison — returns no usable finding for this country (no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice recorded), so where a detained trans visitor would be housed is simply unknown; with no legal gender recognition, the absence of any documented placement standard cannot be read as a protected one.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

Regional framing: the 2016 ruling was the region's first decriminalisation ruling, and at the country's 2018 UN human-rights review it accepted 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations — the first member of its regional grouping to accept that many — pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection, with two rights-equality recommendations noted rather than accepted.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
No LGR; violence in the main city is a general risk.

Prison axis: the only prison-axis source (an online-encyclopaedia survey, fetched HTTP 200) is thin for this country — it records no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units and no solitary/segregation practice, and its only mention of this country is a navbox taxonomy link on general violence — so no usable placement finding exists, and that absence is the finding, not a signal of safety.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the highest national court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — the largest city hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in the largest city happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (the country records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas. The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is a documented law-practice gap: under the national judiciary council's Resolution 348 (13 Oct 2020, amended 2021) a person is recognised as LGBTI for custody purposes by self-declaration before a judge, the judge fixes the place of detention in a reasoned decision after consulting the person's preference, must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit and within it the general population or specific wings or cells, records the declared preference (with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat), and may not use LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation; yet the only subnational census in these sources — 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed inside eleven units treated as masculine across one subnational unit (April–June 2021) — found them housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement documented as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Dating-app robbery schemes (documented as fatal for gay men) are a caution for trans visitors using apps.

Custody framework context: the national placement framework (Resolution 348/2020, amended 2021) is judiciary-level machinery rather than a visitor-facing protection, and the census documenting birth-sex practice was produced with a lead author inside the LGBTI health division of a subnational penitentiary administration — the gap between norm and practice is documented from inside the system.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The name/gender-marker change procedure and the transphobia criminalisation are resident-facing legal machinery; the world's-highest trans murder toll falls on local trans people, concentrated in poor and marginalised communities.

The custody practice is resident-facing: the subnational census (138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed in eleven units treated as masculine, April–June 2021) documents travestis and trans women housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement framed as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations; subnational law has since 2015 granted them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics), and the national norms let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine — a visitor meets all of it only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
The country's general crime problem (armed robbery, express kidnappings, gang violence) drives all governments to advise a high degree of caution for every traveller.

Prison axis: enforcement of the national framework is documented only to the extent of the one subnational census (2021); no source in this record tracks whether other subnational units follow the Resolution's consultation and placement rules, and no data on solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners appears — the ban on using LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation is the norm on paper (Art. 11, VI–VII), not documented practice.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the national human-rights act and the criminal code's hate-crime provisions (2017 reforms); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; national documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (the authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; a national advocacy organisation documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and two provinces have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 national survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical. For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets; the current sources report no marriage or partner-travel friction.

The consequence axis of an arrest is among the most protective documented: since the 2017 reforms banned discrimination based on gender identity, transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, and transgender prisoners imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery; the documented litigation — a transgender prisoner's court proceedings over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution — shows placement and care are litigable in the national courts. The caveats are documented practice gaps: a 2022 news report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in the country's jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault; a 2022 study of correctional officers in one province found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; and no special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail is on record beyond the national identity-based placement rule. For the rare visitor who ends up in custody, the documented standard is identity-based placement with functioning judicial recourse — the abuse allegations are the practice gap to weigh.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Adjacent climate: the 2017 protections were framed as national leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash, and the resident-facing school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks in two provinces are the visible policy turbulence in an otherwise settled national framework.

Custody-axis policy context: the head of government's promised review of transgender prison assignment to ensure facilities match gender identity is national administrative machinery rather than a visitor-facing protection.

Litigation history on the custody axis: an online encyclopaedia's article on a prominent lawyer records that she represented a transgender prisoner in litigation concerning gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution — evidence that trans-prisoner placement and gender-affirming care were litigated in court, though the source gives no dates or final outcome, so the case is thin on specifics. Outside the prison axis, no litigation flux is reported in the current sources: the 2012 human-rights shadow submission predates the 2017 protections (gender identity/expression added to the human-rights act and criminal code; conversion-therapy prohibitions from 2021/22) and is superseded.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Provincial self-declaration legal gender recognition, the national X marker, and the school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks in two provinces are resident-facing; the 2022 survey data describes residents.

The current sources add resident-facing legal infrastructure: a 2016 provincial reform created a document-update pathway (self-declaration plus a doctor's letter, the surgery requirement removed); provincial human-rights commission policy guidance supports sexual-orientation discrimination complaints; the 2012 shadow submission documented the era's trans-protection gaps.

The custody findings are resident-facing: the national identity-based placement rule, the 12-month sex-reassignment-surgery consideration, and the documented conditions (a 2022 correctional-officer study in one province finding officers generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with concerns about risk to other prisoners; a 2022 news report alleging a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners and higher sexual-assault victimisation) govern or describe residents held in custody — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention, and the litigation is a prisoner's case.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals; the current sources do not address marriage or partner-travel questions for a visitor in any detail.

Unverifiable in the current sources: the 2024 national hate-crime analysis page and the 2022 national survey page were not retrievable at research time (redirect loop; timeout), so the figures above rest on the record's summary text and the retrievable source claims.

Prison axis: no special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail is on record beyond the national identity-based placement rule; the abuse allegations in the 2022 news report are reported allegations rather than adjudicated findings; and the litigation's dates and final outcome are not given in the source, so its precedential weight is unverifiable.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by an international equality index and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024). The national government adopted the country's first action plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction, and there is no rollback movement.

The consequence axis of an arrest is only partly documented. Detention law is subnational: the one explicit placement rule on record is a detention law (adopted 13 November 2019), whose separation provisions require female and male detainees to be separated and stipulate that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, with the prison directorate allowed to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. No national placement rule, trans-prisoner case law, special trans unit or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record, so placement for a detained trans visitor is a subnational question that is otherwise undocumented — and detention under a standard with no national guarantee and an explicit deviation power cannot be assumed to follow identity-based placement in every subnational unit.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Same-sex marriage legal since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Placement-framework context: detention law is subnational, and a November 2019 inclusion of gender identity in one subnational unit's detention law — the only such rule documented in this record — was a subnational-level measure aimed at protecting transgender people's placement in correctional facilities; an online-encyclopaedia overview records the vote but documents no national placement rule, so the institutional signal is subnational rather than a visitor-facing national protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The self-declaration LGR process (binary only, no non-binary marker) and the employer duty of care are resident-facing administrative/employment law.

The documented detention rule is resident-facing: the 2019 detention law governs detainees held in that subnational unit, requiring separation of female and male detainees with the caveat that the detained person's gender identity is respected as far as possible and that the prison directorate may deviate in consultation with the referring authority — a standard resident prisoners stand under; a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention, and outside that subnational unit no placement standard is documented.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
The country's principal travel risks (mountain hazards and road safety) affect all travellers.

Prison axis: the 2019 law applies only to one subnational unit; no national trans-prisoner placement rule, trans-prisoner case law, special trans unit or solitary/segregation practice is documented, so placement practice in the other subnational units and the practical operation of the 'as far as possible' standard and its deviation power are unverifiable here — a gap that cannot be read as a protected standard.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city.

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: the only prison-axis source in this record — an international human-rights organisation's country page — contains no document, case or report on transgender prisoners, nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary/segregation practice in the country's prisons. In a country with no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection and an inadequate police response to organised targeting, an undocumented placement practice cannot be read as a protected one: a detained trans visitor would be held in a prison system with no documented housing standard and no documented recourse.
rewrites.blindTangential: Reputation and regional context: long considered the region's tolerant outlier, the country's standing is now in sharp downshift. A regional rights framework exists — a regional resolution marking a decade of advancing LGBT+ rights — though its protective operation here is not evidenced in this record.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Resident-facing data: a 2015 academic study of trans-feminine people (travestis) found they face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and they have been underserved by the country's rights groups, which distanced themselves.

The 2023 official report recorded three community deaths in the year and a transgender man beaten while walking in a suburb of the largest city; it also notes authorities handled complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

The prison-axis documentation gap is itself resident-facing: no rule, case or report on where trans detainees are housed (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in any source in this record — the international human-rights organisation's country page contains no such finding — so detained trans residents stand under an undocumented practice that no source describes as protective.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
The main late-2024 reporting on the hunt wave was not retrievable at research time — the news article returns a hard error — so the wave's details rest on the source summary and corroborating official reporting. A freshness flag notes that criminalisation language cited in 2023-era reports no longer appears in the current overview; whether such provisions persist is unresolved and needs rechecking.

Prison axis: the only prison-axis source is thin — the international human-rights organisation's country page has no usable finding on where trans detainees are housed ('LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link, and no publication from that organisation is listed on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice in the country's prisons) — and with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, that absence cannot be read as a signal of any protected placement standard.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is workable for trans visitors — the region's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via a regional human-rights court's advisory opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively.

Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the majority church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. The capital has a visible scene.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented as a policy-practice gap: since June 2017 the justice ministry has announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility — relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, with a census of self-identified trans prisoners ordered and an exclusive module for trans people under consideration. The practice side diverged: a June 2019 investigation found a trans woman serving a ~6-year sentence at a men's facility, where the prison offered only two options — 'you're a man or a woman here' — and she recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape at another facility that a custodian witnessed; the justice ministry then counted 23 transgender people in the national system. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a formal identity-based choice policy whose documented practice still placed trans women in men's facilities in 2019, with violence and custodial inaction.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Marriage equality since 2020 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

The 2017 placement policy was presented as modelled on another country's system, with protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with a civil-society legal organisation since 2016 — institutional context for the choice policy rather than a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The administrative name/photo ID process (which does not change the sex marker) and universal healthcare covering transition-related care are resident-facing.

The custody policy and its documented practice are resident-facing: the 2017 justice-ministry choice policy (voluntary placement by gender identity, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, census ordered, exclusive module considered) and the 2019 counter-example — a trans woman serving ~6 years at a men's facility who said the prison offered only 'man or woman' and recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape at another facility witnessed by a custodian — govern prisoners; a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
ID sex-marker limits and church influence are resident-facing/climate.

Prison axis: no data on trans special units or solitary/segregation practice is documented — the exclusive module was 'under consideration' in 2017 and whether it was ever built is unverifiable from these sources; how the 2017 choice policy operates today is likewise unverified, with the 2019 men's-facility placement the only documented practice point.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution from trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016, and the legal framework is now among the region's strongest. The 2024 reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the identity document directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery), and in 2024-25 court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate government response, and the 'internal armed conflict' against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024, with two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks; the two main cities carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis. For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.

The consequence axis of an arrest is the record's darkest documented element. Trans women in the country's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces: the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all the country's prisons (an organisation working with them says there are many more), placement operates by birth sex/legal sex, and the protective priority pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations is used unevenly — one trans detainee was initially sent to a male pavilion with three other trans women rather than to it, and received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The sources document gender-identity discrimination, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers in custody, including the death of a trans woman during the November 2021 massacre at a prison while held in a male prison space, a 2022 complaint over cruel and degrading treatment of trans women in another prison, 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving and beatings targeting breast/body implants, a 2026 death in custody of a 23-year-old trans woman that drew calls for an independent investigation, and reporting that rapes and torture in custody are directed at prisoners' gender identity. The leading trans-rights organisation does not push a one-size placement rule — it advocates individualised housing decisions per regional human-rights standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, citing a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty — so a detained trans visitor would face male-space placement under an unevenly applied protective standard with documented violence.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The framework's bedrock is the adjacent layer: the 2008 constitution's non-discrimination foundation (including sexual orientation and identity), the 2019 marriage-equality ruling, and a 2018 court order requiring the civil registry to register the child of a same-sex couple. Dated official context: a 2011 human-rights report documented discrimination based on sexual orientation among broader societal problems, and the platform notes that same-sex couples remain barred from adoption by a constitutional ban.

Custody-framework context: the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty predates the documented placement practice, and the leading trans-rights organisation's prison program deliberately advocates individualised housing decisions under regional human-rights standards rather than a single placement rule — institutional context for the documented male-space practice, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The 2024 civil-registry reform and the adolescent document-change rulings are resident-facing; the 27-murder toll and its inadequate government response fall on residents.

The adolescent rulings arose from a specific teenager's case that opened the path for other adolescents seeking legal recognition, and the 2024 reform's operative procedure came via the 2024 regulation of the identity law.

The documented custody conditions are resident-facing: trans women held in male pavilions, the protective priority placement used unevenly, and the documented deaths and abuse (the November 2021 massacre death at a prison while held in a male space, the 2022 complaint over treatment in another prison, the 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving and beatings, the 2026 death in custody at a maximum-security prison) all fall on residents held in the system — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
The general security emergency affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific legal/violence balance. The murder toll is a single organisation's documentation and the response assessment is that organisation's; the 2024-25 adolescent rulings are as reported and not independently re-verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

Prison axis: the census count (73 trans women) and the priority-pavilion practice are as reported by the cited investigations — how allocation to the protective pavilion is decided and how many trans women reach it is not documented, the implementation status of the 2016 protocol commitment is unverified, and no rule or case law fixing trans-prisoner placement (birth-sex vs identity) is on record beyond the documented practice itself.
